meta.ogDescription: Real and sourceable: Orwell's dropped 1945 preface to Animal Farm, unpublished until the Times Literary Supplement printed it on 15 September 1972.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real and sourceable. It is the closing argument of “The Freedom of the Press,” the preface Orwell wrote for Animal Farm around 1945 — an essay that was dropped from the book and stayed unpublished until the Times Literary Supplement printed it on 15 September 1972 ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Orwell’s proposed preface to Animal Farm, written c. 1945 and omitted from the first edition (Secker and Warburg, 17 August 1945)
TLS: The Times Literary Supplement (London), 15 September 1972, with an introduction by Bernard Crick

source.excerpt: If liberty means anything at all it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.
trail: Quote Investigator is the anchor and its finding is unambiguous: Orwell wrote a preface to Animal Farm circa 1945, it was rediscovered in 1971 among books owned by Roger Senhouse, it was published in the TLS in 1972, and the quotation about liberty appeared within it ↗. QI also logs the line running in James Reston’s New York Times column of 24 September 1972, days after the TLS printing.

The Orwell Foundation — an independent charity licensed by the Orwell Estate — hosts the essay in full and dates its first appearance precisely: the Times Literary Supplement, 15 September 1972, introduced by Sir Bernard Crick ↗. Reading it there puts the sentence in the closing movement of Orwell’s argument rather than on a poster.

Accounts of the find differ slightly, and it is worth saying so. QI dates the rediscovery to May 1971 in Senhouse’s books; Wikipedia’s Animal Farm article credits Ian Angus with rediscovering the typescript in 1972 ↗. Both agree on the essay, the author, and the 15 September 1972 TLS publication.

Wikiquote lists it among the sourced quotations, not the misattributed ones, tying it to the original 1945 preface to Animal Farm ↗ and separately flagging the loose paraphrase that circulates alongside it.
source.cutTag: c. 1945 · the preface that was cut
source.excerptNote: In the essay the sentence lands at the end of a paragraph aimed squarely at Orwell’s own literary class: he says he knows the arguments by which the English intelligentsia justify their timidity, asks for no more talk of defending liberty against Fascism, then delivers this line — adding that ordinary people still roughly believe it and act on it. Read the surrounding paragraph in the full text of the essay ↗.

source.rightsNote: “The Freedom of the Press” was written around 1945 but not published until 15 September 1972, which keeps it in copyright in the US until roughly 2067. In the UK and EU, Orwell’s copyright expired on 1 January 2021 — 70 years after his death — so the text is public domain there. The Orwell Foundation still reproduces it under permission from the Estate: “this material remains under copyright and is reproduced here with the kind permission of the Orwell Estate” ↗. Quoting the single sentence with attribution is ordinary fair use anywhere; reproducing the whole essay is not.
source.useLine: Still under copyright in the US (rights held by The Orwell Estate) until roughly 2067; in the UK and EU it has been public domain since 1 January 2021, 70 years after Orwell’s death. A short, credited quote is fine anywhere for talks, teaching, and internal decks; for commercial, published, or large-scale reuse outside the UK and EU, get permission.

author.name: George Orwell
author.heading: Who was George Orwell?
author.bio: Born Eric Arthur Blair in Motihari, British India, in 1903, Orwell spent his career writing against comfortable lies — as a colonial policeman turned tramp, a militiaman in Spain, a wartime BBC broadcaster, and finally the author of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four. He is the rare writer whose politics cut in every direction: a democratic socialist who spent as much ink on the self-deceptions of the English left as on fascism. He died of tuberculosis in London in January 1950, months after Nineteen Eighty-Four made him famous.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — Orwell really wrote it. What circulates wrongly is the source, plus a family of shortened rewrites that get passed off as his.

items.why: A 1987 reference work, The Wit and Wisdom of the 20th Century: A Dictionary of Quotations, printed a compressed version and pointed the citation at The Road to Wigan Pier. Quote Investigator searched The Road to Wigan Pier itself and could not find the quotation anywhere in it ↗.

items.who: “Freedom is the right to tell people what they do not want to hear”
items.why: A tidied-up version that keeps Orwell’s name. Quote Investigator concludes it “probably evolved from the quotation with the word ‘liberty’,” and that there is no substantive evidence Orwell penned the variant ↗.

items.who: “Liberty is telling people what they do not want to hear”
items.why: Wikiquote records this as a paraphrase of the sourced line ↗, not as anything Orwell wrote. If you want his words, use the full nineteen-word sentence.

Printings genuinely differ, and the comma is the later form. The Orwell Foundation’s text ↗ and Quote Investigator’s transcription of the 1972 TLS printing ↗ both have no comma; the comma shows up in James Reston’s New York Times column of 24 September 1972, in later quotation books, and in the wall inscription outside Broadcasting House as Wikipedia renders it. Nothing turns on it; the wording is otherwise identical.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is authentically Orwell’s, and it has a real address: the final paragraph of “The Freedom of the Press,” his rejected preface to Animal Farm, first published in the Times Literary Supplement on 15 September 1972 ↗.

context.heading: Why Orwell wrote it — and why nobody read it for decades
lead: Orwell wrote the line not about tyrants abroad but about his own side. Animal Farm was an anti-Stalin fable written while Stalin was Britain’s wartime ally, and Orwell had been turned down by publisher after publisher who found the allegory impolitic. The preface was his answer: an attack not on state censorship but on the voluntary kind — editors, publishers and intellectuals who suppressed criticism of the Soviet Union because it was awkward rather than because it was untrue.

Then the preface itself got cut. Space had been allotted for it in the author’s proof, and its removal forced a last-minute renumbering of pages before Secker and Warburg published the first edition on 17 August 1945 ↗. An essay arguing that unwelcome speech must be printable was, fittingly, the part of the book that did not get printed.
context.detailsSummary: The line’s second life: carved outside the BBC
detailsBody: The sentence is now Orwell’s most public words in Britain. Martin Jennings’s statue of Orwell was unveiled outside Broadcasting House on 7 November 2017 ↗, and Wikipedia records that “the wall behind the statue is inscribed with George Orwell’s words ‘If liberty means anything at all, it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear’, from an unused preface to Animal Farm.”

Orwell had worked for the BBC himself during the war, in the Indian Section of its Eastern Service — a detail that gives the choice of wall a certain edge, since the essay carved on it is about institutions declining to broadcast inconvenient things.
context.pull: An essay about voluntary censorship was itself quietly cut from the book.
